### An Effective Intraday Momentum Strategy for S&P500 ETF (SPY)

May 14, 2024
...
Our experience as practitioners tells us that markets can exhibit much shorter bursts of directional movement, often within the trading day. What makes this particularly interesting, from a research standpoint, is determining whether these moves are simply noise or something genuinely exploitable.

In this paper, we focus on SPY, one of the most widely traded and closely observed ETFs in the world, and investigate whether abnormal intraday demand–supply imbalances can be captured using a systematic trend-following framework.

Our signal detection begins by defining what we call the noise area: a time-varying equilibrium zone built from SPY’s average absolute move from the open at each intraday timestamp over the previous 14 sessions.

These historical average moves define an upper and lower boundary around the day’s opening level, so that the threshold required to signal imbalance is typically narrower early in the session and wider later in the day.

In other words, these bands are designed to separate ordinary market oscillation from abnormal buying or selling pressure. As long as price stays within that zone, we assume the market is in equilibrium and the strategy stays flat. Only when price breaks above or below those boundaries do we treat the move as evidence of a genuine intraday trend worth acting on.

title: Out-of-Sample Evaluation of an Intraday Momentum ...
snippet:
Zarattini, Aziz, and Barbon (2025) present an intraday momentum strategy for SPY that achieves an annualized return of 19.6% and a Sharpe Ratio of 1.33 over the period 2007-2024. This paper independently replicates their strategy using IQFeed 1-minute data and evaluates its performance on approximately two years of out-of-sample data (May 2024 to March 2026). Our in-sample replication closely matches the original results, confirming the reproducibility of the strategy (Sharpe Ratio 1.34 over 2015-2024). However, out-of-sample performance deteriorates substantially: the strategy achieves a total return of only 9.4% versus 29.5% for a passive buy-and-hold, with a Sharpe Ratio of 0.39. The decline in risk-adjusted returns is statistically significant. We examine potential explanations for this degradation, including changing market microstructure, the proliferation of zero-days-to-expiration (0-DTE) options, and the possibility that the observed underperformance falls within historical drawdown norms. Our findings highlight the importance of out-of-sample validation for intraday trading strategies and contribute to the ongoing discussion about the persistence of momentum anomalies at high frequencies.

title: Intraday Momentum -- Researched based strategy deep dive, part 1
snippet:
This strategy is based on the research found in references Maróy's 1 & Zarattini's 2. Both of them discuss the same strategy, but reference 1 is the newer paper that attempts to expand on and improve the original strategy. The purpose of this test is to see if there is an efficacy to the strategy idea. Maróy's paper uses several different methods to improve on the original paper, but it is highly optimized and only has results on 1 instrument in a short time period for back testing results. With that in mind, my goal is to recreate the logic from the papers and then see if we can make it more robust and applicable to more instruments.

Before testing this logic on the 1-minute or 1-second chart (used in Maróy's paper), I want to do a fast and dirty check of the logic using a daily historical chart. The purpose is to create a simple daily strategy that uses the same concepts from the paper to see if there is any reason to continue down to intraday time periods for further investigation.

So, let's summarize the main points of the paper and create a strategy in RealTest (RT) that has similar logic. We will use QQQ for this test, since that is the test the most recent paper decided to focus on. I will use historical returns to create the volatility bands and then set the strategy to take positions only if a bar crosses the upper or lower band.
